label: Losing a Child
framing: There is no grief like the death of a child, the loss that breaks the order of things and leaves a parent burying the one they were meant to raise. Scripture does not flinch from this sorrow, recording the wail of David and the inconsolable weeping of Rachel, and it makes no attempt to explain it away, only to hold the grieving inside a love that does not let go.
cultural: Our culture has few words for the parent who has lost a child and often pulls away, awkward and afraid, leaving the bereaved more alone in the cruelest season of their lives. The biblical world grieved loudly and together, tearing clothes and sitting in ashes for days, refusing to hurry the mourner along, and naming the loss for exactly the catastrophe it is.
historical: Jacob, in the patriarchal age, refused all comfort when he believed his son was dead, saying he would go down to the grave mourning. The Christian writers have walked this valley with the bereaved across the centuries, and few more honestly than Nicholas Wolterstorff, the philosopher who lost his son on a mountain in 1983 and wrote his lament not to resolve the grief but to keep faith with it.
application: Do not let anyone rush you or measure your grief, for this loss is carried for a lifetime, not a season. Let your church bring meals, sit in silence, and speak your child's name without fear. Lean on a counselor or a grief group of other bereaved parents, and on your pastor, and pray the laments when prayer is all you have left. The hope of resurrection does not cancel the grief, but it means the goodbye is not the last word.

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”
verses.where: In a chapter full of promises of homecoming, a mother's lament breaks in: Rachel, the mother of the tribes, weeping for children who are no more and refusing to be comforted. God does not rebuke her. He answers her in the next two verses, and the answer is hope for her future, not an order to stop grieving.

verses.text: “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”
verses.where: Herod has the boys of Bethlehem killed, and Matthew tells it in one sentence and then gives the mothers' grief a whole verse of Scripture. He names Herod's rage as the cause and does not say the killing happened so that Scripture would be fulfilled. He does not explain why one child was saved and the others were not, and it is honest to say so.

verses.text: All his sons and daughters tried to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. “No,” he said. “I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” So his father wept for him.
verses.where: Jacob is shown his son's robe dipped in blood and believes Joseph is dead. He tears his clothes, mourns many days, and refuses every attempt to comfort him, saying he will go down to the grave mourning. The Bible lets that grief stand for years of the story without hurrying it.

verses.text: David answered, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’ But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
verses.where: David fasts and lies on the ground for seven days while his infant son is ill, and when the child dies he rises, worships and eats. The text ties this death to David's own sin, and the site's note does not soften it; it is one hard story, and Jesus later refused to read other deaths that way (John 9:3; Luke 13:4). Many Christians have taken comfort from David's words, “I will go to him,” as hope of reunion; others take them to mean only that David too will die.

verses.text: “Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? After all, the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me.”
verses.where: Naomi left Bethlehem with a husband and two sons and comes home with neither. When the women of the town greet her by name, she tells them to call her Mara, bitter, because she went away full and came back empty. The book keeps her bitterness in her own words and goes on to show God's kindness working toward her before she can see it.

verses.text: so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed— and a sword will pierce your soul as well.”
verses.where: At the happiest moment of Mary's life, when her baby is presented in the temple, Simeon tells her that a sword will pierce her soul. Most readers take it as the grief she would carry when her son was rejected and killed; she stood near his cross. The mother of Jesus is among the parents who watched a child die.

verses.text: When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said, “Do not weep.”
verses.where: At the gate of Nain a funeral is coming out: the only son of a widow. No one asks Jesus for anything. He sees the mother first, his heart goes out to her, and then he raises her son. The site's note is careful: if no miracle came for you, the story does not mean you were loved less; it shows who Jesus is, the Lord who sees the grieving and is stronger than death.

verses.text: Then Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped, saying: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.”
verses.where: Job hears in one day that all ten of his children are dead. He tears his robe, falls to the ground and worships, and the narrator says he did not sin in what he said. The book does not end there. Two chapters later he curses the day he was born, and at the end God says Job spoke rightly of him where his comforters did not.

verses.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.
verses.where: David teaches what he learned when God answered him. The same psalm admits that the afflictions of the righteous are many, so this is not a promise that grief will be short. It is a statement about where God is: near the brokenhearted, close enough to save those whose spirit is crushed.

verses.text: I will rejoice in Jerusalem and take delight in My people. The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her. No longer will a nursing infant live but a few days, or an old man fail to live out his years. For the youth will die at a hundred years, and he who fails to reach a hundred will be considered accursed.
verses.where: God promises new heavens and a new earth, a city where weeping is no longer heard. The first loss the prophet names as gone is a nursing infant who lives only a few days. Readers differ on how the rest of verse 20 fits the final state, but on every reading God names the death of a child as something his new world will not contain.

misread.taken: Grieving parents are often told, sometimes at the graveside, that all things work together for good, as if the death of their child were itself good, or part of a plan they should be able to see and accept by now.
misread.says: Paul does not call suffering good. The “all things” in this chapter include famine, danger and sword, and Paul says only that none of them can defeat God's purpose. He defines the good in the next verse as being made like Christ, not as an explanation of any one loss. The site's note on the chapter says it plainly: this is never a line to hand to someone in fresh grief. It is a hope a grieving person may come to hold, in their own time, not a sentence anyone may use to close their mouth.
misread.text: And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose.

whole: If the weight of this is more than you can bear today, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a grief counselor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The death of a child breaks the order of things. Parents are meant to be buried by their children, not to bury them. The house goes quiet in a way nothing else makes it quiet, the birthdays keep coming, and an ordinary question about how many children you have becomes hard to answer. The world around you moves on in weeks while you have barely begun, husbands and wives often grieve differently and can drift apart without meaning to, and brothers and sisters carry their own grief, often quietly.

Scripture does not explain this loss away, and it does not ask parents to. It keeps Rachel refusing to be comforted, Jacob mourning a son he thought was dead, Naomi asking to be called bitter, and David at the city gate crying out, “If only I had died instead of you.” It tells of Mary standing near the cross of her own son. The Bible treats death as an enemy, the last one to be destroyed, and the death of a child is that enemy at its most unnatural. Nothing in Scripture lets anyone tell a parent that their child's death was deserved. When people asked Jesus whether suffering and sudden death were punishment, he said no.

That shapes what wisdom looks like here. It refuses the easy sentences, including true verses spoken too soon. It lets grief take as long as it takes, and it expects the second year to be hard. It names the child and remembers them out loud. It asks the church to weep with those who weep, and to keep doing it long after the funeral, when the casseroles have stopped. It tells a parent that anger and questions can be brought straight to God, as Job and the psalmists did, and that seeking help from a counselor or a doctor, or from other parents who have buried a child, is not a lack of faith. And it reminds every Christian that God is not a stranger to this grief. The Father gave his own Son, and the Son wept at a grave.

The hope Scripture gives is real, and it does not shorten the grief. Jesus at Nain saw the mother before he did anything else, and he raised her son because he is stronger than death. The promise for all who are his is the resurrection, and a new creation where, in Isaiah's words, no nursing infant lives only a few days. God told weeping Rachel that there was hope for her future. Parents who believe it still ache every day. Grief and hope can live in the same heart, and the God who is near to the brokenhearted does not ask you to choose between them.
deep.sit: What is one thing about your child you want someone to remember with you, and who could you tell it to this week?

prayer.lead: Psalm 88 is the darkest prayer in the Bible, and the man who prayed it still called God the God of his salvation and kept praying. You may pray it on the days when nothing else will come.
prayer.text: O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You. May my prayer come before You; incline Your ear to my cry.

careLines.text: If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like Rachel's, you are allowed to refuse comfort for a time, as she did.
Please do not carry it alone.
Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.
Your grief is not a lack of faith.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
